module.title: Loading & Performance
module.description: Weight and balance fundamentals, performance calculations, and factors affecting UAS flight characteristics

lessons.title: General Loading and Performance
objectives: Explain how added weight affects endurance, range, climb, and maneuverability
Use bank angle and load factor to find the load an aircraft must support
Identify the Part 107 weight limit and where an aircraft's loading limits come from

sections.title: The Core Weight-Performance Principle
sections.content:
## What This Covers

Every drone has limits. How much it can carry, how long it can stay airborne, how well it climbs, and how it handles are all determined by its weight and the conditions it is flying in.

## The Core Principle

**More weight = more lift required = more power required = less performance.**

To stay level, an aircraft must produce lift equal to its weight. Add weight and the motors must work harder, which draws more current and drains the battery faster.

## Where the Limits Come From

The manufacturer sets the maximum weight and the balance limits for the aircraft. The remote PIC is responsible for loading it within those limits and for knowing how the loading affects performance.

When no manufacturer data exists, build experience with the aircraft cautiously and stay well inside what it has shown it can do.

## What to Know

- Adding payload always reduces flight time
- Being under the maximum weight keeps the aircraft within limits. It does not preserve the published no-payload performance
- A small unmanned aircraft under Part 107 weighs **less than 55 pounds** on takeoff, including everything on board or attached

sections.title: How Payload Affects Flight Characteristics
sections.content:
## Endurance (Flight Time)

Every bit of payload makes the motors work harder and draw more current from the battery. Flight time goes down.

## Range

Range decreases with added weight because the aircraft uses its battery faster and covers less ground before it must return.

## Climb Rate

A heavier aircraft climbs more slowly, because more of the available power is used just to stay airborne.

## Maneuverability

A heavier aircraft responds more slowly to control inputs and takes more room and more time to stop, turn, or recover.

## Fixed-Wing Aircraft: Stall Speed and Takeoff

For a fixed-wing sUAS, more weight means:

- A **higher stall speed**
- A longer takeoff run and a higher landing speed
- A reduced rate of climb

## Altitude and Heat

In thin air, propellers and wings produce less lift. An aircraft that hovers easily at sea level with a full payload may struggle with the same load at a high-elevation site on a hot day. Weight and density altitude work against you together.

bogeyman.message: Added payload costs endurance. Every time.

sections.title: Load Factor in Turns
sections.content:
## What Load Factor Is

Load factor is the load the aircraft's structure and wings must support, compared with the aircraft's weight. It is expressed in G.

- In straight and level, unaccelerated flight the load factor is **1 G**: lift equals weight.
- In a level turn, part of the lift is used to turn the aircraft, so total lift must increase to hold altitude. The load factor rises with **bank angle**.

## Load Factor in a Level, Coordinated Turn

| Bank angle | Load factor |
|---|---|
| 0° | 1.0 |
| 30° | about 1.15 |
| 45° | about 1.41 |
| 60° | 2.0 |

The load factor does not depend on the aircraft's weight or speed, only on the bank angle. It rises slowly at first and steeply beyond 45°.

## Working a Load Factor Question

**Load supported = weight × load factor**

A 10-pound fixed-wing sUAS in a level 45° banked turn: 10 × 1.41 = about **14 pounds**.

The same aircraft at 60° of bank: 10 × 2.0 = **20 pounds**.

On the test, the load factor for a given bank angle is read from a chart in the testing supplement. Find the bank angle, read across to the load factor, and multiply by the weight.

## Why It Matters

- **Stall speed increases** as load factor increases. An aircraft that flies comfortably wings-level can stall in a steep turn at the same airspeed.
- The structure must carry the extra load. A heavily loaded aircraft in a steep turn can exceed what it was built for.
- For multirotors, any hard maneuver demands more thrust. A heavily loaded aircraft has less thrust in reserve.

## Common Traps

- "A 60° bank doubles the stall speed." It doubles the **load**. Stall speed rises, but by less than double.
- "Load factor depends on how heavy the aircraft is." The factor depends on bank angle. The load in pounds depends on both.

bogeyman.message: Bank angle sets the load factor. Weight times load factor gives the load. At 60 degrees of bank, the wings are carrying twice the aircraft's weight.

sections.title: Key Facts and Common Traps
sections.content:
## Key Facts to Memorize

| Fact | Detail |
|---|---|
| Part 107 weight limit | Less than 55 lbs on takeoff, including everything on board or attached |
| Lift and weight | In level flight, lift must equal weight |
| More weight | Shorter flight time, slower climb, less maneuverability |
| Fixed-wing | More weight means a higher stall speed |
| Load factor at 60° bank | 2 G |
| Thin air | Compounds the effect of weight, because less lift is available |

## Common Traps

### Trap 1: Published Flight Time

"The drone is rated for 25 minutes, so it will fly 25 minutes with the camera on."

❌ Wrong. The published figure is for the published weight and conditions. Added payload shortens it.

### Trap 2: Under Maximum Weight Equals Safe

"The drone is under its maximum takeoff weight, so it's safe to fly."

❌ Not necessarily. High density altitude can leave an aircraft short of performance even at a legal weight, and the balance limits must be met too.

### Trap 3: Weight Improves Stability

"More weight makes the drone more stable and easier to handle."

❌ Wrong. More weight means slower response and less performance in reserve.

bogeyman.message: More weight needs more lift, and more lift needs more power. Published flight time is for the published weight.

lessons.title: Effects of Loading Changes
objectives: Explain how battery depletion affects performance during flight
Describe temperature effects on loading performance
Understand altitude effects on payload capacity
Relate weight to stall speed for fixed-wing sUAS

sections.title: Battery Consumption During Flight
sections.content:
## What Happens as the Battery Discharges

A fuel-burning aircraft gets lighter as it flies. A battery-powered aircraft does not: **a discharged battery weighs the same as a charged one**.

What changes is the electrical power available.

### Voltage Falls

As a lithium battery discharges, its voltage drops. Less power is available to the motors late in the flight than at the start.

### Demand Peaks Hurt More

A climb, a gust, or a hard maneuver asks for a burst of power. Late in the flight the battery is less able to deliver it.

## The Bottom Line

Performance **degrades** as the battery discharges. Expect:

- Less power available
- Lower climb capability
- Less margin for wind and maneuvering

Plan the demanding parts of a flight for early in the battery, and land with a reserve.

bogeyman.message: A battery weighs the same empty as full. What changes during the flight is the voltage, and it only goes down.

sections.title: Temperature Effects on Performance
sections.content:
## How Temperature Affects Performance

Temperature works on a drone in two ways: through the battery and through the air.

### Cold Weather

- Battery capacity and power output are reduced
- Flight time is shorter than the published figure
- Keep batteries warm before flight and follow the manufacturer's temperature limits

### Hot Weather

- Hot air is less dense, so propellers and wings produce less lift
- Motors and batteries run hotter
- More power is needed to do the same work

## The Double Penalty

On a hot day the air is thinner, so the aircraft needs more power to hover, while heat is also working against the battery and motors. That is why a hot day at a high-elevation site is so demanding.

## Where to Find the Limits

The manufacturer's manual gives the operating temperature range for the aircraft and its batteries. Stay inside it.

sections.title: Altitude Effects on Loading
sections.content:
## How Altitude Affects Loading

As altitude increases, air density decreases.

### The Effects

- Propellers produce less thrust per revolution
- Motors must spin faster to produce the same lift
- Power consumption increases and flight time falls
- The payload an aircraft can lift is reduced

## Combined Effects

High elevation and high temperature both thin the air. Together they are worse than either one alone. Density altitude, covered in the next lesson, puts the two into a single number.

## Fixed-Wing sUAS: Loading and Stall Speed

For fixed-wing drones, weight directly affects stall speed:

**Heavier aircraft stall at higher airspeeds.**

Adding payload raises the stall speed, so the aircraft must fly faster to stay airborne, which increases the power it needs.

### Key Relationship

| Loading | Stall Speed |
|---|---|
| Increased weight | Higher stall speed |
| Decreased weight | Lower stall speed |

sections.title: Common Traps
sections.content:
## Common Traps

### Trap 1: Weight Loss During Flight

"The drone gets lighter as the battery drains, so performance improves."

❌ Wrong. A battery does not lose weight as it discharges, and falling voltage reduces the power available.

### Trap 2: Independent Effects

"Temperature and altitude effects are independent."

❌ Wrong. Both reduce air density. A hot day at high elevation is worse than either condition alone.

### Trap 3: Constant Payload Capacity

"The drone can carry its full rated payload at any altitude."

❌ Wrong. Less lift is available in thin air, so the payload it can carry is reduced.

## Key Facts to Memorize

| Fact | Detail |
|---|---|
| Battery weight | Does not change during the flight |
| Battery voltage | Falls as the battery discharges, reducing available power |
| Cold | Reduces battery capacity and output |
| Heat and elevation | Both reduce air density and lift |
| Stall speed and weight | Heavier = higher stall speed (fixed-wing) |

lessons.title: Balance and Center of Gravity
objectives: Define center of gravity and explain why it matters
Compare effects of forward vs aft CG
Distinguish between static and dynamic stability
Explain CG limits and their importance

sections.title: What is Center of Gravity?
sections.content:
## Center of Gravity Definition

The **center of gravity (CG)** is the single point where the aircraft's total weight is balanced. If you could hang the drone from one point and have it sit perfectly level, that point is the CG.

## Why CG Matters

Even if your drone is within its total weight limit, **where** that weight is positioned matters enormously. An unbalanced drone can be uncontrollable.

## Critical Fact: CG is Not Fixed

The CG shifts whenever you:
- Add or remove payload
- Reposition payload

A battery weighs the same charged or discharged, so the CG does not move during an ordinary flight unless something shifts or is released.

## The Core Concept

A drone can be within its total weight limit but **outside its CG limits**. Both limits must be satisfied for safe operation.

sections.title: Forward CG (Nose-Heavy)
sections.content:
## Forward CG Effects

When the CG is forward of the ideal position:

### For Multirotors

- The front motors must produce more thrust to hold the nose up, and the rear motors less
- The hard-working motors draw more current and run hotter
- Flight time is reduced, and there is less control margin in the direction the aircraft is being held

### For Fixed-Wing sUAS

- The tail must produce more downward force to balance the nose
- That downward force acts like added weight, so the wing must produce more lift
- **Stall speed increases**
- Drag increases, so cruise is less efficient
- The aircraft is **more stable in pitch**, but heavier on the controls and harder to flare for landing

## The Trade-off

**Forward CG = more stable but less efficient**, for a fixed-wing aircraft within its limits.

Forward of the limit, the aircraft may not have enough elevator authority to raise the nose.

bogeyman.message: For a fixed-wing aircraft, forward CG is stable but inefficient: higher stall speed, more drag. You pay for the stability with performance.

sections.title: Aft CG (Tail-Heavy)
sections.content:
## Aft CG Effects

When the CG is aft of the ideal position:

### For Multirotors

- Rear motors work harder; front motors loaf
- Aircraft tends to pitch backward
- Oscillations in pitch axis become more pronounced
- Flight time is reduced, and there is less control margin

### For Fixed-Wing sUAS

- Less tail downforce needed, so less drag (more efficient)
- **Stall speed decreases** (aircraft can fly slower)
- But pitch stability is reduced — oscillations may grow instead of dampen
- Recovery from unusual attitudes becomes difficult
- **Dangerous condition** — can lead to loss of control

## The Danger

**Aft CG = less stable, potentially dangerous**

While aft CG is more efficient, the reduced stability is a real safety concern.

bogeyman.message: Aft CG is efficient but less stable. Aft of the limit, the aircraft can become uncontrollable.

sections.title: Lateral CG and CG Limits
sections.content:
## Lateral CG (Side-to-Side Balance)

If payload is mounted off-center (left or right), one side's motors must work harder:

- Continuous correction required to maintain level flight
- Motors on the heavy side overheat
- Power consumption rises and flight time falls
- In extreme cases, the overworked motors reach maximum output and the drone rolls toward the heavy side

## CG Limits

Manufacturers specify a CG range (e.g., 95 mm to 115 mm from the nose reference).

### Operating Outside CG Limits Means:

- The aircraft may be uncontrollable
- Published performance data is invalid
- The operation is unsafe regardless of total weight

## The Fact to Remember

A drone can be within its total weight limit but outside its CG limits. **Both limits must be satisfied** for safe operation.

| Condition | Safe to Fly? |
|---|---|
| Within MTOW, within CG limits | ✅ Yes |
| Within MTOW, outside CG limits | ❌ No |
| Over MTOW, within CG limits | ❌ No |
| Over MTOW, outside CG limits | ❌ No |

sections.title: Static vs Dynamic Stability
sections.content:
## Two Types of Stability

These are two distinct concepts:

### Static Stability

The aircraft's **initial** response to a disturbance.

- **Positive static stability:** After a gust pushes the nose up, the aircraft initially tends to pitch back down toward level. This is desirable.
- **Negative static stability:** After a gust pushes the nose up, the aircraft continues pitching up. This is dangerous.

**Forward CG increases positive static stability; aft CG decreases it.**

### Dynamic Stability

Whether oscillations after a disturbance **grow or shrink** over time.

- **Dynamically stable:** Oscillations get smaller over time. The aircraft settles back to equilibrium.
- **Dynamically unstable:** Oscillations grow larger. Even if the aircraft initially tries to correct, the overcorrections build until control is lost.

## A Scenario

> "An aircraft is disturbed by a gust. It initially pitches back toward level but then oscillates with increasing amplitude."

This describes an aircraft that is **statically stable but dynamically unstable** — it tries to correct but overcorrects each time.

Reduced stability of this kind is associated with a CG too far aft.

bogeyman.message: 'Initially returns toward level, but the oscillations grow' = statically stable, dynamically unstable.

sections.title: CG Summary and Traps
sections.content:
## Key Facts to Memorize

| Fact | Detail |
|---|---|
| Forward CG | More stable, higher stall speed, less efficient |
| Aft CG | Less stable, lower stall speed, potentially dangerous |
| CG shifts when | Payload is added, removed, or repositioned |
| Static stability | Initial tendency to return to equilibrium |
| Dynamic stability | Whether oscillations grow or shrink over time |
| CG limits | Must be within range regardless of total weight |

## Common Traps

### Trap 1: Weight-Only Thinking
**"The drone is under MTOW, so CG doesn't matter."**

❌ Wrong. CG can be out of limits even at reduced weight.

### Trap 2: Responsive = Stable
**"More responsive means more stable."**

❌ Wrong. Responsiveness indicates reduced stability.

### Trap 3: Efficiency First
**"Aft CG is more efficient, so it's always better."**

❌ Wrong. Aft CG reduces stability and can lead to loss of control.

### Trap 4: Confusing Stability Types
**Mixing up static and dynamic stability.**

An aircraft can be statically stable but dynamically unstable — know the difference.

lessons.title: Performance Data and Density Altitude
objectives: Interpret manufacturer performance data and its limitations
Calculate density altitude using the standard formula
Apply density altitude to flight planning decisions

sections.title: Understanding Manufacturer Data
sections.content:
## Manufacturer Performance Data

Typical specifications a manufacturer provides:

| Data Point | What It Tells You |
|---|---|
| Maximum Takeoff Weight (MTOW) | Total weight including airframe, battery, and payload |
| Payload capacity | Maximum external load weight |
| Flight time | Endurance at specified conditions |
| Maximum speed | Top ground speed |
| Climb rate | Vertical speed capability |
| Wind resistance | Maximum sustainable wind speed |
| Operating temperature range | Safe ambient temperature limits |

## The Fine Print: Test Conditions

Published figures are measured under specific conditions that the manufacturer chooses, typically favorable ones: low elevation, mild temperature, little wind, a new battery, and a balanced load.

Read the manual for the conditions behind each number. Real operations rarely match them, so expect less than the published figure when it is hot, high, windy, or the aircraft is loaded.

## Where to Look First

For the performance and loading limits of a particular aircraft, the first source is the **manufacturer's manual or published specifications**. The AIM and the sectional chart contain no aircraft-specific data.

bogeyman.message: Can you count on the published specs on a hot day at elevation? No. Expect less, and plan for it.

sections.title: What is Density Altitude?
sections.content:
## Density Altitude — The Key Performance Tool

Density altitude is the single most important concept in this section. It answers the question:

**"What does the air think the altitude is?"**

## Definition

**Density altitude** is pressure altitude corrected for non-standard temperature. It tells you the equivalent altitude at which the air has the same density as your actual conditions.

## Why It Matters

Your drone doesn't care about your actual elevation. It cares about **air density**.

On a hot day at moderate elevation, the air may be as thin as it would be at a much higher altitude. Your drone performs as if it's at that higher altitude.

## Pressure Altitude vs. Density Altitude

| | Pressure Altitude | Density Altitude |
|---|---|---|
| **Based on** | Barometric pressure only | Pressure + temperature |
| **Used for** | Altimeter settings, airspace | **Performance calculations** |
| **Accounts for temperature?** | No | Yes |

**For any question about aircraft performance, use density altitude — never pressure altitude.**

sections.title: Calculating Density Altitude
sections.content:
## The Formula

**Density Altitude = Pressure Altitude + (120 × Temperature Deviation in °C)**

### Where:

- **Pressure Altitude** = Field Elevation + ((29.92 − Current Altimeter Setting) × 1,000)
- **Temperature Deviation** = Actual Temperature (°C) − Standard Temperature (°C) for that altitude
- **Standard Temperature** at sea level = 15°C, decreasing approximately 2°C per 1,000 feet

## Standard Temperature Reference

| Altitude (ft) | Standard Temp (°C) | Standard Temp (°F) |
|---|---|---|
| Sea level | 15°C | 59°F |
| 1,000 | 13°C | 55°F |
| 2,000 | 11°C | 52°F |
| 3,000 | 9°C | 48°F |
| 4,000 | 7°C | 45°F |
| 5,000 | 5°C | 41°F |
| 6,000 | 3°C | 37°F |
| 7,000 | 1°C | 34°F |
| 8,000 | −1°C | 30°F |
| 9,000 | −3°C | 27°F |
| 10,000 | −5°C | 23°F |

## Memory Aid: The Lapse Rate

Standard temperature decreases about **2°C per 1,000 feet** (the "lapse rate").

sections.title: Density Altitude Examples
sections.content:
## Worked Example 1: Hot Day at Moderate Elevation

**Given:**
- Airport elevation: 3,000 feet MSL
- Altimeter setting: 29.92" Hg (standard)
- Outside air temperature: 35°C (95°F)

**Step 1 — Pressure Altitude:**
Since altimeter setting is standard (29.92), pressure altitude = field elevation = **3,000 ft**

**Step 2 — Temperature Deviation:**
- Standard temp at 3,000 ft = 9°C
- Actual temp = 35°C
- Deviation = 35 − 9 = **+26°C**

**Step 3 — Density Altitude:**
DA = 3,000 + (120 × 26) = 3,000 + 3,120 = **6,120 feet**

**What this means:** Your drone will perform as if it's at 6,120 feet, even though you're standing at 3,000 feet. Expect less endurance and climb performance than the published figures.

---

## Worked Example 2: High Altitude Operation

**Given:**
- Airport elevation: 7,000 feet MSL
- Altimeter setting: 29.80" Hg
- Outside air temperature: 25°C (77°F)

**Step 1 — Pressure Altitude:**
PA = 7,000 + ((29.92 − 29.80) × 1,000) = 7,000 + 120 = **7,120 ft**

**Step 2 — Temperature Deviation:**
- Standard temp at 7,000 ft = 1°C
- Actual temp = 25°C
- Deviation = 25 − 1 = **+24°C**

**Step 3 — Density Altitude:**
DA = 7,120 + (120 × 24) = 7,120 + 2,880 = **10,000 feet**

**What this means:** The air is much thinner than at sea level, and payload capacity is reduced.

sections.title: Favorable Conditions Example
sections.content:
## Worked Example 3: Cool Day (Favorable Conditions)

**Given:**
- Airport elevation: 5,000 feet MSL
- Altimeter setting: 30.10" Hg
- Outside air temperature: 0°C (32°F)

**Step 1 — Pressure Altitude:**
PA = 5,000 + ((29.92 − 30.10) × 1,000) = 5,000 + (−180) = **4,820 ft**

**Step 2 — Temperature Deviation:**
- Standard temp at ~5,000 ft = 5°C
- Actual temp = 0°C
- Deviation = 0 − 5 = **−5°C**

**Step 3 — Density Altitude:**
DA = 4,820 + (120 × (−5)) = 4,820 − 600 = **4,220 feet**

## What This Means

Cold air is denser than standard. The density altitude is **lower** than field elevation.

Your drone performs better than the elevation would suggest — as if it were at 4,220 feet instead of 5,000.

**However:** Remember that cold temperatures reduce battery performance, so the aerodynamic advantage may be offset by reduced battery output.

sections.title: High, Hot, and Humid
sections.content:
## The Three Enemies of Performance

A simple memory aid for density altitude and performance:

- **High** elevation = less air density
- **Hot** temperature = less air density
- **Humid** air = slightly less air density (a smaller effect than the other two)

All three increase density altitude and reduce performance.

## Worst-Case Scenario

**A high-elevation airport on a hot, humid summer afternoon.**

This is when you'll see:
- Maximum density altitude
- Minimum payload capacity
- Shortest flight times
- Most reduced climb performance

## Memory Aid

**"High, hot, and humid = horrible performance."**

bogeyman.message: HIGH + HOT + HUMID = the worst possible conditions for drone performance. All three factors INCREASE density altitude and REDUCE what your drone can do.

sections.title: Using Performance Data for Flight Planning
sections.content:
## Pre-Flight Performance Planning

Before every flight, a remote PIC should:

1. **Determine density altitude** for current conditions
2. **Consult the manufacturer's data** for performance and limits
3. **Allow a margin** below the published figures for real-world conditions
4. **Verify weight and balance** are within limits as loaded
5. **Plan mission duration** with a battery reserve

14 CFR 107.49 requires the remote PIC to ensure there is enough power for the intended operating time.

## Battery Reserve

Plan to land with charge in hand. A reserve covers:

- Unexpected wind on the way back
- A return-to-home or a go-around
- A battery that delivers less than expected

## Other Performance-Limiting Factors

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| Cold batteries | Reduced capacity and power output |
| Aging batteries | Reduced capacity compared with new |
| Wind | Headwinds reduce range and groundspeed; gusts increase power consumption |
| Propeller condition | Nicked or worn propellers reduce thrust and add vibration |
| Payload imbalance | Off-center loads make some motors work harder and increase power consumption |

sections.title: Performance Data Traps
sections.content:
## Key Facts to Memorize

| Fact | Detail |
|---|---|
| DA formula | PA + (120 × temp deviation in °C) |
| Standard sea-level temp | 15°C (59°F) |
| Lapse rate | ~2°C per 1,000 feet |
| Performance tool | Always use density altitude, not pressure altitude |
| Manufacturer specs | Measured under the manufacturer's test conditions — expect less in the field |
| High, hot, humid | All increase DA and reduce performance |
| Safety margin | Allow a margin below published figures; land with a battery reserve |

## Common Traps

### Trap 1: Wrong Altitude Type
**Using pressure altitude for performance questions.**

❌ Wrong. Always use **density altitude**.

### Trap 2: Wrong Temperature Units
**Forgetting to convert °F to °C.**

The formula uses Celsius. If the question gives Fahrenheit:
**°C = (°F − 32) × 5/9**

### Trap 3: Trusting Specs
**Thinking manufacturer specs are guaranteed.**

❌ They apply to the manufacturer's test conditions. Expect less when it is hot, high, or windy.

### Trap 4: Ignoring Altimeter Setting
**Forgetting to correct pressure altitude.**

If the altimeter setting is not 29.92, you must correct the pressure altitude before calculating density altitude.

### Trap 5: Dismissing Humidity
**"Humidity doesn't matter."**

Humidity has a smaller effect than temperature or altitude, but it does increase density altitude slightly.

bogeyman.message: Any question about aircraft performance calls for density altitude, not pressure altitude.
